If the numbers don't match, call your plan first, then the No Surprises Help Desk at 1-800-985-3059 with both papers in hand. In most cases, the No Surprises Act protects you from a surprise anesthesia bill after planned care at an in-network facility. That covers an out-of-network anesthesiologist at an in-network hospital, hospital outpatient department or ambulatory surgical center, if you use most types of private health insurance. CMS lists anesthesiology among the specialties that are not allowed to ask you to sign away that protection. Based on CMS pages we read in full on November 28, 2026, the protection has firm limits. Ground ambulances generally fall outside it. So do short-term limited duration plans, health care sharing ministries and fixed indemnity plans. A bill can still be correct. If the amount matches the Patient Balance on your explanation of benefits (EOB), it equals what CMS calls the amount you owe after your insurer has paid everything else. If the bill is higher, CMS points you to your provider, your plan and the No Surprises Help Desk at 1-800-985-3059. Tools for this journey On This Page Can You Be Billed More Than In-Network Rates? For emergency care, CMS states the limit outright: if your plan covers emergency care, you can't be charged more for emergency medical services than the in-network cost-sharing rate. That limit applies to the hospital, the providers treating you at the hospital, and an air ambulance provider that took you to the hospital. CMS defines cost-sharing as a copayment, deductible or coinsurance. For planned, non-emergency care, CMS uses different wording on its rights page for people using insurance . In most cases, you're protected from unexpected out-of-network bills for non-emergency care related to a visit to an in-network hospital, hospital outpatient department or ambulatory surgical center. CMS gives the example of a local hospital that is in-network. An out-of-network anesthesiologist at an in-network surgery center fits that example. CMS names anesthesiology, radiology, pathology, and diagnostic and laboratory services among the specialties that are not allowed to ask you for a notice and consent form. Those providers can't get you to sign away the balance billing protections for that care. Your coverage type decides whether any of this applies. The protections cover insurance through an employer (including a Federal Employees Health Benefits plan), the federal Health Insurance Marketplace, a State-based Marketplace or other individual market coverage. The law took effect on January 1, 2022. CMS also notes that some health plans don't cover emergency care. If you're unsure what your plan covers, contact your insurance company before assuming the emergency limit applies. The disagreement over an out-of-network payment amount belongs to the provider and your plan. CMS describes its consumer protections as removing consumers from payment disagreements between providers, health care facilities and health plans. Its October 2021 rules set up an independent dispute resolution (IDR) process to settle those payment amounts between providers and plans. What the No Surprises Act Covers and Does Not The No Surprises Act covers emergency care, air ambulance services and planned care at in-network hospitals, hospital outpatient departments and ambulatory surgical centers, and it leaves out ground ambulances and several plan types. The next section covers that exception. Two rows change the answer for an anesthesia bill. If your procedure happened in a doctor's office that is not a hospital outpatient department, the planned-care protection does not reach it. If the facility itself was out-of-network, the protection for planned care at in-network facilities does not apply either. Medicare, Medicaid, Indian Health Services, Veterans Affairs Health Care and TRICARE get a separate row. CMS says only that these plans already protect you from some unexpected out-of-network bills. For a billing issue under one of them, CMS offers an action plan tool that asks a few questions about your bill. When Signing a Consent Form Gives Up Your Protection A notice and consent form is the document that can give up your No Surprises Act protection, and CMS heads that topic with the warning that signing one may increase your costs. CMS says an out-of-network provider may ask you to sign one for post-stabilization services after an emergency room visit. Signing it means you give up your billing protections for that care. For planned care at an in-network facility, a valid form can waive the protection for some scheduled care from an out-of-network provider. The form also can't be used when no in-network provider is available. A shortage of in-network providers bars the form. The answer flips for a provider outside the CMS list. If you signed a valid form for a provider who is allowed to ask, that provider's out-of-network bill can fall outside the protection. When someone hands you a form, look at who is asking. If the provider is on the list below, CMS says they are not allowed to ask, and if you want to keep your protection, don't sign. If you already signed one, keep the signed and dated copy, because CMS lists it among the documents to include with a complaint. CMS lists these specialties as not allowed to ask you for a notice and consent form: Anesthesiology Radiology Pathology Diagnostic and laboratory services Emergency medicine Neonatology Assistant surgeons Hospitalists Intensivists What Viral Surprise Anesthesia Bill Scripts Get Wrong Viral surprise anesthesia bill scripts get the core protection right and the follow-up tools wrong. They tell patients to rip up their bills and mix up the rules for insured and uninsured patients. One post pushing the rip-it-up tactic passed 4,100 likes on November 28, 2026, and copycat step-by-step threads are spreading. No CMS page we read tells you to ignore, tear up or throw away a medical bill. The CMS pages tell you to compare the bill with your EOB, contact your plan and submit a complaint when the rules aren't followed. The good faith estimate is the first mix-up. CMS limits it to people who don't have health insurance or don't use it to pay for care. Usually, those patients get a written estimate when they schedule care at least 3 business days in advance or ask for one. An uninsured or self-pay patient may dispute a bill that is at least $400 more than the good faith estimate from that same provider, and the dispute has a 120-day window to start. Each estimate covers a single provider or facility, so CMS's surgery example calls for 2 estimates, one from the surgeon and one from the hospital. There is no estimate during emergency care. If you used insurance, the $400 dispute is the wrong tool. Your route runs through the EOB, your plan and the No Surprises Help Desk. Ground ambulances are the other mix-up. CMS says ground ambulance services generally aren't covered by the Act's billing protections unless a state law has different rules. A script that promises federal relief on a ground ambulance bill gets this wrong. Some scripts also overstate what an insured patient can refuse. If the bill is higher than your EOB Patient Balance, CMS says to talk to your provider, and a bill that matches your EOB Patient Balance is the amount CMS says you owe after your insurer pays. How to Check a Surprise Anesthesia Bill Step by Step Check a surprise anesthesia bill by matching it against your EOB, calling your plan, and filing a complaint if the numbers still don't match. The steps follow CMS guidance, and the one practical step we added is marked as ours. An EOB isn't a bill. It shows Provider Charges, the amount your provider bills, and Allowed Charges, the amount your provider will be paid. It also shows Paid by Insurer and the Patient Balance, which CMS calls the amount you owe after your insurer has paid everything else. The EOB shows what you owe, and it does not show whether you already paid part of it. A remark code of 2 or 3 letters and numbers explains costs, and the bottom of the EOB describes each code. The online complaint form resets after 15 minutes of inactivity, so photograph your documents before you start. You can return later with your confirmation number to add more documents. CMS also points to state Consumer Assistance Programs and patient advocates on its page about checking a bill for errors . If the bill matches the Patient Balance, it is the amount CMS says you owe after your insurer has paid everything else. Our guide to payment plans and hospital financial assistance covers a balance you can't afford. If you pay from a health savings account (HSA) or flexible spending account (FSA), the HSA and FSA reimbursement checklist lists the records to keep. Work through these steps in order: Ask the provider's billing department for a detailed bill that lists the cost of each medical item or service. Get your EOB and find the Patient Balance. CMS says on its EOB guide that your bill should not be higher than the Patient Balance, and if it is, talk to your provider. Compare the bill with your medical records and look for double billing, which CMS says is especially common when more than one provider treated you. You shouldn't get a bill for anything not documented in your records, and some providers charge a records fee. Call your plan at the phone number printed on the EOB. CMS says your insurance company might be able to fix billing errors with your provider. Ask the plan to review the claim as care covered by No Surprises Act protections. This is a practical step we suggest, and CMS itself says only to contact your plan. Gather your documents: the medical bill, a photo of your insurance card and the EOB, plus any signed notice and consent form, letters with the provider, appeal decisions and evidence of coverage. Submit a complaint to the No Surprises Help Desk online or at 1-800-985-3059, and write down your confirmation number. If the Help Desk needs more information, it will contact you within 60 days. Call 1-800-985-3059 with your confirmation number to check status. Ground Ambulance Bills and State Rules Ground ambulance bills generally fall outside the No Surprises Act, so ground ambulance providers are still allowed to charge out-of-network rates and cost-sharing unless state law says otherwise. CMS's ground ambulance action plan applies if you got an unexpected bill, used health insurance and were taken to the hospital by ground ambulance. If you were billed in one of the states listed below, CMS suggests calling the ground ambulance provider. Tell them you're aware of surprise billing rules for ground ambulance services, because they may be able to reduce your bill. Outside those states, ask for a lower bill or a payment plan. CMS says providers or their billing departments can sometimes lower the price and may offer payment plans. The state list is dated November 15, 2021, and current rules in your state may differ. A Consumer Assistance Program in the state where you got care may be able to give advice for your specific case, and CMS links to those programs from the same ground ambulance action plan. Patient advocates and a friend or family member who can speak for you are the other help CMS lists. CMS lists these 10 states with ground ambulance billing protections as of November 15, 2021: Colorado Delaware Florida Illinois Maine Maryland New York Ohio Vermont West Virginia Our Takeaway If you have private insurance and an out-of-network anesthesiologist, radiologist, pathologist or lab billed you after care at an in-network hospital, hospital outpatient department or ambulatory surgical center, the No Surprises Act generally protects you. Those specialties are not allowed to ask you to waive that protection. Compare the bill with the Patient Balance on your EOB, call your plan, and file with the No Surprises Help Desk at 1-800-985-3059 if the bill is higher. Based on CMS pages we read in full on November 28, 2026, this is a reported synthesis of federal guidance for most private plans. It is not a test of any provider or plan. If you're uninsured or paying yourself, use a good faith estimate and the $400 dispute instead of the EOB route. If the bill came from a ground ambulance, a doctor's office that is not a hospital outpatient department, an out-of-network facility, or a short-term, sharing ministry or fixed indemnity plan, the federal protection does not cover it. For a ground ambulance bill, ask the provider for a lower bill or a payment plan. **Conditions:** Applies to people using most private health insurance: employer plans including Federal Employees Health Benefits plans, the federal Health Insurance Marketplace, State-based Marketplaces and other individual market coverage. Planned-care protection covers care related to a visit to an in-network hospital, hospital outpatient department or ambulatory surgical center. The explicit in-network cost-sharing limit is CMS wording for emergency care only. Medicare, Medicaid, Indian Health Services, Veterans Affairs Health Care and TRICARE already protect you from some unexpected out-of-network bills. **What would change this answer:** The answer changes if CMS or Congress revises the covered settings or the notice and consent exceptions, if you signed a valid notice and consent form for a provider allowed to ask for one, if your EOB shows the billed amount equals your Patient Balance, if a state ground ambulance law covers the bill, or if you did not use insurance, which moves you to the good faith estimate route. Frequently Asked Questions What if my anesthesiologist is out of network? If you used most types of private insurance and the anesthesiologist treated you at an in-network hospital, hospital outpatient department or ambulatory surgical center, the No Surprises Act protects you from unexpected out-of-network bills in most cases. CMS says anesthesiologists are not allowed to ask you to sign a notice and consent form. Compare the bill with your EOB Patient Balance and call your plan if the bill is higher. Can I be billed more than in-network rates at an in-network hospital? For emergency care, CMS says the hospital, its providers and an air ambulance provider can't charge more than the in-network cost-sharing rate if your plan covers emergency care. For planned care, CMS says you're protected from unexpected out-of-network bills in most cases. That protection can end if you signed a valid notice and consent form for a provider who is allowed to ask for one. Does the good faith estimate apply if I have insurance? No. CMS limits the good faith estimate to people who don't have insurance or choose not to use it. Those patients may dispute a bill at least $400 more than that provider's estimate, while insured patients use the EOB, their plan and the No Surprises Help Desk. Are ground ambulances covered by the No Surprises Act? Generally, no. CMS says ground ambulance providers are still allowed to charge out-of-network rates and cost-sharing unless state law says otherwise, and it listed 10 states with protections as of November 15, 2021. Ask the ground ambulance provider for a lower bill or a payment plan. Who do I call about a surprise medical bill? Call your health plan first, using the phone number on your EOB, because CMS says the plan might be able to fix billing errors with your provider. If the problem continues, call the No Surprises Help Desk at 1-800-985-3059. CMS offers phone support 7 days a week in English, Spanish and over 350 other languages. What if I signed a consent form? A signed notice and consent form can give up your protection for care from a provider who is allowed to ask for one. CMS says anesthesiology, radiology, pathology, diagnostic and laboratory services, emergency medicine, neonatology, assistant surgeons, hospitalists and intensivists are not allowed to ask. Keep the signed and dated form and include it if you submit a complaint. Can surprise medical bills go to collections? The CMS pages we read on November 28, 2026 do not address collections. Call the No Surprises Help Desk at 1-800-985-3059 to ask about your situation. Keep your bill, EOB and any complaint confirmation number together. Does the No Surprises Act apply to Medicare or Medicaid? CMS says Medicare, Medicaid, Indian Health Services, Veterans Affairs Health Care and TRICARE already protect you from some unexpected out-of-network bills. For a billing issue under one of these plans, CMS offers an action plan tool and the No Surprises Help Desk at 1-800-985-3059. Putting a medical bill on a credit card out of panic strips away protections that apply to healthcare debt. Converting an outstanding balance into commercial credit turns medical collections into ordinary consumer debt subject to immediate credit bureau reporting. Taking deliberate, sequenced action protects your personal budget. This guide breaks down the legal rights, hospital requirements, and practical negotiation steps that keep medical obligations from derailing your finances. Tools for this journey Budget calculator → Credit card payoff → Personal loans → Snowball vs avalanche → What to Do First When a Medical Bill Arrives Do not pay a medical balance immediately upon receiving the first billing statement. Medical bills frequently contain coding errors, duplicate charges, or services that an insurance carrier should have covered under the policy terms. Call the provider and request an itemized bill showing every specific procedure code and medication fee. Once that document arrives, pull the explanation of benefits (EOB) issued by your health insurance company for those dates of service. Compare each line item to ensure the provider credited your insurance adjustments and that you are only being billed for the copayment, coinsurance, or deductible amount verified by the insurer. Check whether the billing violates the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) No Surprises Act , which took effect January 1, 2022. This federal statute protects patients from surprise out-of-network bills for emergency services, non-emergency care provided by out-of-network clinicians at in-network hospitals, outpatient departments, or ambulatory surgical centers, and air ambulance transportation. If you are an uninsured or self-pay patient, providers generally must provide a good faith estimate when scheduled at least 3 business days ahead, and you can formally dispute a bill that exceeds that estimate by $400 or more by calling the CMS help desk at 1-800-985-3059. For a bill from an out-of-network anesthesiologist, radiologist or lab after care at an in-network facility, see the No Surprises Act protections for a surprise anesthesia bill before you arrange payment. Setting Up an Extended Medical Bill Payment Plan Most healthcare providers will agree to split an outstanding balance across regular monthly installments rather than demanding the entire sum at once. Ask the billing department directly for an interest-free arrangement before discussing any other payment method. Consider a hypothetical worked example of a $6,000 hospital bill. If the provider agrees to a zero percent payment plan stretched over 24 months, the required payment comes out to exactly $250 a month ($6,000 divided by 24). Whether a specific hospital or physician group offers zero percent terms is entirely up to their internal policies, which makes asking directly necessary. Always secure the agreed terms in writing before making an initial payment. Confirm that the agreement specifies zero percent interest, lists the fixed monthly due date, and explicitly states that the account will remain in good standing without referral to third-party collection agencies so long as you meet the schedule. You can test how different monthly installments fit your broader cash flow using our budget calculator . Hospital Financial Assistance and Charity Care Deadlines Nonprofit hospitals are legally required to maintain written financial assistance policies that reduce or eliminate bills for qualifying patients. Under Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Section 501(r)(6) , charitable hospitals must make reasonable efforts to determine whether an individual qualifies for financial help before initiating extraordinary collection actions. Extraordinary collection actions include reporting the debt to credit reporting agencies, selling the account to outside debt buyers, or pursuing judicial proceedings such as a lawsuit. The statutory framework grants patients specific timeframes anchored to the initial billing statement: A 120-day notification period starts on the date of the first post-discharge billing statement, and the hospital must send written notice at least 30 days before the end of that period describing the collection actions it may take. A 240-day application period opens on that same first post-discharge billing statement date, during which you can submit a financial assistance application. Request the facility's plain-language summary of its financial assistance policy, along with the application form. Each hospital sets its own eligibility rules, so ask for the written policy and read the income limits before you apply. How to Negotiate Medical Bills Directly You can negotiate medical bills directly with the hospital or clinic billing manager without outside help. Providers often accept a discounted lump-sum settlement if you offer to pay immediately. Begin by contacting the billing office and explaining your cash constraints plainly. Ask if the office offers a prompt-pay discount for self-pay balances, which often reduces the total fee by a noticeable margin if settled within a short window. If you cannot afford a lump sum, request that the provider reprice your charges to match the rates they accept from major insurance carriers. If your total disputed balance runs into tens of thousands of dollars and involves complex surgical bills, hiring an independent medical bill advocate can be worth considering. A professional advocate audits medical records and challenges improper coding on your behalf. The operational decision criterion for hiring an advocate is straightforward: consider one if the disputed balance exceeds several thousand dollars and you lack the time to audit technical hospital billing codes yourself. For standard balances, direct negotiation preserves your cash. Risks of Using Credit Cards and Personal Loans Transferring an unpaid medical balance onto a credit card or commercial loan eliminates the unique consumer protections built specifically into healthcare debt. Once you swipe a credit card or accept a medical loan, the debt belongs to a private financial lender under standard consumer credit contracts. If you leave the medical bill with the clinic, you retain access to statutory charity care programs, zero-interest internal payment schedules, and strict credit bureau reporting pauses. Moving that balance to a credit card creates high-interest revolving debt where a missed payment is reported under standard credit rules. If you are already struggling with high-interest card debt, you can calculate the payoff timeline on our credit card payoff calculator . There is one concrete inversion case where borrowing money makes sense: when an independent provider refuses to perform a non-emergency, medically necessary procedure without advance payment, offers no internal financing, and the interest on an unsecured loan is manageable. In that narrow scenario, reviewing a medical loan or checking borrowing terms on our personal loan hub can secure needed treatment, provided you have exhausted all charity care options first. Credit Reporting Rules and Protections for Medical Debt Medical debt operates under different credit reporting standards than credit cards, mortgages, or auto loans. Equifax , Experian , and TransUnion maintain voluntary reporting policies that protect consumers from sudden credit damage while resolving healthcare disputes. Under these voluntary bureau standards, paid medical collection accounts do not appear on credit reports, and unpaid medical collections under $500 are entirely excluded from credit reporting. The bureaus also wait 365 days before new medical debt can appear on a credit report. This one-year window allows time to file insurance appeals, negotiate adjustments, or complete charity care reviews. Regulatory history is important here because enforcement rules shifted recently. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) finalized a rule under Regulation V in January 2025 designed to prohibit consumer reporting agencies from including any medical debt on credit files. However, the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Texas vacated that rule in July 2025 in Cornerstone Credit Union League v. CFPB. As a result, the comprehensive federal ban is not in effect, and consumer protection currently relies on the voluntary credit bureau policies. Nonprofit Relief and Income-Based Hardship Programs Patients struggling with major medical bills can access outside relief programs designed to cover out-of-pocket healthcare expenses. These programs help bridge the gap when insurance benefits expire or when household income exceeds standard hospital charity care thresholds. Disease-specific charitable organizations provide targeted grants to individuals diagnosed with chronic, rare, or life-altering conditions. These non-profit foundations frequently distribute dedicated co-pay assistance, travel grants for specialized treatment, and subsidies for daily maintenance medications. Independent religious charities and community-based nonprofit groups also offer emergency financial assistance funds to prevent utility shutoffs or evictions caused by medical distress. When exploring local assistance, contact hospital social workers directly, as clinical case managers regularly maintain rosters of active regional patient relief funds. Tax Deductions for Medical Expenses Medical expenses can provide tax relief, but the Internal Revenue Service limits how many taxpayers can actually benefit from the deduction. Under IRS Topic 502 , medical and dental expenses are deductible only to the extent that they exceed 7.5% of your adjusted gross income (AGI), and only if you itemize deductions on Schedule A of Form 1040. Consider a hypothetical worked example with an AGI of $80,000. The 7.5% baseline threshold equals $6,000 ($80,000 multiplied by 0.075). If you incur $9,000 in qualifying medical bills during the calendar year, only the $3,000 spent above the $6,000 floor counts as a deductible expense. Under the IRS 2026 inflation adjustments , the standard deduction is $16,100 for single filers and $32,200 for married couples filing jointly. Itemizing deductions solely to claim $3,000 in excess healthcare expenses rarely beats taking the standard deduction unless you possess extensive additional itemized deductions. Qualified deductible costs can include capital expenses for medical care. According to IRS Publication 502 , home modifications made for medical care, such as access ramps, widened doorways, or support grab bars, count as a deductible medical expense only to the extent the cost exceeds any increase in the home's market value. Handling Medical Debt Collectors When a medical provider gives up on internal billing, they transfer or sell the unpaid account to a collection agency. Third-party collectors are governed by the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) and federal rules outlined on the CFPB debt collection page . If your bill has been forwarded to an outside agency, review our guide on how to deal with debt collectors to understand your communication rights. Follow this checklist when managing collection notices: Request written validation of the debt to verify the underlying provider, date of service, and itemized balance. Do not provide verbal bank account access or authorize automatic debit transactions over the phone. Verify whether the balance is under $500, because the major credit bureaus exclude unpaid medical collections below that threshold from credit reports. Negotiate a single lump-sum settlement in writing before sending funds if you choose to pay, ensuring the agreement confirms the debt is satisfied in full. Understanding your rights prevents collection agencies from coercing you into unfavorable payment structures. You can prioritize medical settlements alongside other obligations by studying how to pay off debt across structured repayment plans. When Standard Medical Debt Strategies Do Not Apply The steps in this guide do not apply to non-medical consumer debt, nor do they help individuals who already transferred hospital balances to private credit cards or personal loans. If you converted your medical balance to commercial credit, you must use standard debt repayment strategies such as the debt snowball vs avalanche method . Our advice to negotiate before borrowing would change if the credit bureaus dropped their voluntary medical debt policies or if a provider refused every payment plan and demanded payment up front. To begin resolving your balance today, call your healthcare provider's billing office to request a detailed itemized bill and a financial assistance application before agreeing to any repayment terms. Frequently asked questions How do I deal with medical debt I can't afford to pay? Request an itemized bill, compare it to your insurer's explanation of benefits, and apply for the hospital's financial assistance policy. Nonprofit hospitals must offer charity care to qualifying patients under federal tax law, and setting up an interest-free payment plan keeps the debt out of collections. Can I negotiate a hospital bill? Yes, you can negotiate hospital bills directly with the facility's billing department. Providers routinely offer prompt-pay discounts for lump-sum settlements, lower rates to match commercial insurance payments, or set up zero percent multi-year installment agreements upon request. Is medical debt on my credit report? Medical debt does not appear on your credit report if it is paid, if the unpaid balance is under $500, or if it is newer than the bureaus' 365-day waiting period. The three nationwide credit bureaus voluntarily exclude paid accounts and sub-$500 collections while providing a one-year grace period for larger balances. Should I put a medical bill on a credit card? No, you should avoid putting medical bills on a credit card whenever possible. Transferring medical debt to credit cards strips away the 365-day credit reporting waiting period, removes charity care access, and replaces potential zero-interest payment terms with high-interest consumer revolving credit. Can I deduct medical expenses on my taxes? You can deduct qualified medical expenses only if you itemize deductions on Schedule A and your total unreimbursed costs exceed 7.5% of your adjusted gross income. Because standard deduction thresholds are high, claiming medical expenses alone rarely produces a tax benefit. A health savings account (HSA) and a health flexible spending arrangement (FSA) handle distributions under different federal tax rules. In the money guides we publish, our approach starts directly with primary rules from the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) . An HSA reimburses qualified medical expenses incurred after the account is established under state law. You keep the records with your tax files rather than submitting every receipt to the government. An FSA generally reimburses qualified expenses incurred during your coverage period and requires third-party substantiation. Some qualifying debit-card transactions need no additional information. Neither account permits double reimbursement. If health insurance or another party paid a portion of the bill, only your remaining out-of-pocket share qualifies for reimbursement. You also cannot claim an itemized medical deduction on Schedule A (Form 1040) for any medical expense paid with tax-free funds from an HSA or an FSA. Tools for this journey IRS Reimbursement Rules → On This Page Reimbursement Checklist Before You File Records for Your Reimbursement Checklist HSA Expense Timing and Recordkeeping FSA Coverage and Substantiation Membership Fees Need a Separate Check Submit One Claim and Save the Result Finish Your Reimbursement Checklist Reimbursement Checklist Before You File Before you request an HSA distribution or submit an FSA claim, walk through these six steps in order: Obtain an itemized bill or provider statement showing the patient name, provider name, date of service, service description, and amount charged. Verify timing against account rules, confirming your HSA was already established when the expense occurred, or that the expense fell within your active FSA coverage period. Subtract all insurance payments, provider discounts, and outside reimbursements to calculate your remaining out-of-pocket responsibility. Check that you have not previously reimbursed this amount through another account or claimed it as an itemized deduction on Schedule A. Match the claim against your specific account requirements, submitting third-party substantiation for an FSA or logging the records into your tax files for an HSA. Save the submission confirmation, administrator response, and actual reimbursement record alongside your itemized invoices. These checks help you identify duplicate payments and missing records before requesting reimbursement. Records for Your Reimbursement Checklist A complete reimbursement checklist relies on documentation that demonstrates what care was provided, who received it, when it occurred, and how much you paid. Do not rely on a generic payment receipt that only lists a total charge. Document field Practical purpose Provider or facility name Identifies the independent party that delivered the care or medical product Patient name Identifies who received the care so you can check beneficiary eligibility Item or service description Helps you assess the medical purpose against the applicable account rules Date of service or purchase Provides the date to compare with account establishment or coverage dates Total charge and patient responsibility Shows the exact unreimbursed dollar amount owed after any adjustments For expenses processed through health insurance, an Explanation of Benefits (EOB) provides helpful documentation. An EOB details what the provider billed, the portion paid by insurance, and your final responsibility. An EOB alone does not serve as proof of payment, so retain your final payment receipt as well. If a bill from an out-of-network specialist looks higher than your EOB, learn how to check an out-of-network specialist bill against your explanation of benefits before you request reimbursement. Keep documentation showing you paid the remaining balance. If an invoice bundles multiple items together, request an itemized statement from your provider so that each individual charge is visible. HSA Expense Timing and Recordkeeping IRS Publication 969 states that an HSA can pay or reimburse qualified medical expenses incurred after the account is established. State law determines when an HSA is established, and a rollover account may inherit an earlier establishment date. Contact your HSA custodian if you need to confirm your formal account establishment records. You do not mail receipts to the IRS when you withdraw money from an HSA. Instead, you report total distributions on Form 8889 with your annual tax return. IRS Publication 969 requires you to keep records in your personal files showing that all distributions paid exclusive qualified medical expenses. Your HSA records must establish three things: The distributions paid or reimbursed qualified medical expenses incurred after the account was established. The medical expenses were not previously paid or reimbursed from another source. You did not claim the expenses as an itemized deduction on Schedule A in any tax year. Expense timing carries one narrow conditional exception. For a qualifying direct primary care service arrangement (DPCSA), IRS Notice 2026-5, question 19 permits three HSA expense dates: The first day of each month of coverage, on a pro rata basis. The first day of the coverage period. The date the fees are paid. This rule generally permits reimbursement of substantiated periodic fees before the associated coverage begins, provided the arrangement satisfies all statutory criteria. That flexibility applies strictly to qualifying arrangements under HSA rules and does not alter timing requirements for an FSA. FSA Coverage and Substantiation A health FSA operates under distinct statutory constraints. IRS Publication 969 explains that health FSA distributions generally reimburse qualified medical expenses incurred during your actual period of coverage. An FSA cannot advance reimburse future or projected expenses. You must receive the medical care before an FSA can issue reimbursement. Plan documents determine whether your employer offers a grace period or carryover provision, so review your plan materials for your specific claim submission deadline. Substantiating an FSA claim requires written statements from an independent third party showing that the medical expense was incurred and listing the exact amount. The employee must also provide a written statement confirming the expense has not been paid or reimbursed by any other health plan. When you use an FSA debit card, certain transactions meeting automated substantiation methods do not require additional documentation. Paying with a card does not guarantee that substantiation is complete, and your plan administrator may still request an itemized invoice. Keep your receipts and substantiation confirmations with your claim records. Membership Fees Need a Separate Check Fixed periodic medical membership fees require careful analysis before you submit a claim or withdraw funds. An itemized invoice or provider marketing statement does not automatically transform a nonqualified membership fee into a qualified medical expense. IRS Publication 502 defines medical expenses to include diagnosis, treatment and prevention of disease, and care affecting body structure or function. The medical purpose still has to meet the applicable HSA or FSA rules. Amounts spent for general health improvement are excluded. If an agreement bundles administrative services, wellness benefits, and clinical access together, request an itemized description of included services from the organization to determine what care was delivered. For HSA reimbursement, IRS Notice 2026-5, question 20 requires solely primary care services from qualifying primary care practitioners. A fixed periodic fee must be the sole compensation for that care. The arrangement cannot include procedures requiring general anesthesia, prescription drugs other than vaccines, or laboratory tests not typically administered in an ambulatory primary care setting. Question 20 notes there is no specific dollar cap on fees eligible for HSA reimbursement under this rule, though contribution eligibility remains separate. Under IRS Notice 2026-5, question 18 , employer-paid DPCSA fees are not expenses of the HSA beneficiary and cannot be reimbursed from the HSA. This includes DPCSA fees paid through salary reduction under a cafeteria plan. A fee that fails the DPCSA conditions does not qualify under this special HSA reimbursement rule. Separately billed medical services still need their own qualification and timing checks. Submit One Claim and Save the Result To file your claim, follow the specific submission steps provided by your account custodian or third-party administrator. For an FSA claim, submit the required third-party statement and no-other-payment certification in the format your administrator requests. For an HSA, follow your custodian's platform instructions to request a distribution. After submitting documentation, retain the following records: The submission confirmation number or upload receipt. A copy of all itemized statements and explanations of benefits provided. The administrator's approval or payment statement. The actual reimbursement record. If your administrator flags an expense due to missing details, request an itemized invoice directly from your medical provider. A confirmation receipt acknowledges that paperwork was received, but it does not guarantee claim approval or tax-free status. Finish Your Reimbursement Checklist Completing a health account reimbursement requires matching verified documents to applicable tax regulations. Start by assembling the itemized records for a single expense, confirm your account establishment date or coverage window, and verify that no other coverage has paid the bill. If an expense involves bundled services, questionable qualification, or incomplete receipts, pause the reimbursement. Review the relevant federal criteria in IRS Publication 969 and IRS Publication 502 before withdrawing funds or filing claims. Take the next action on your reimbursement checklist by requesting an itemized invoice for your most recent unreimbursed medical expense and checking your account timing rules. Frequently Asked Questions Can I reimburse myself out of my HSA? Yes, you can reimburse yourself out of your HSA for qualified medical expenses incurred after the account was established under state law. You must maintain records showing the expenses were not reimbursed by insurance or other sources and were not claimed as an itemized deduction on your tax return. Does HSA reimbursement require a receipt? IRS rules require sufficient records showing that your HSA distribution paid or reimbursed qualified medical expenses. Keep itemized receipts and other records showing the expense was not paid elsewhere or claimed as an itemized deduction. Keep these with your tax records rather than sending them with your return. Can an FSA reimburse an expense before the service happens? No, an FSA cannot advance reimburse future or projected expenses. Under IRS Publication 969, expenses are only eligible for FSA reimbursement after the medical care has actually been provided during your active coverage period. Can I reimburse a medical membership fee? Check the services, payment source and applicable account rules before reimbursing a membership fee. For an HSA, a qualifying DPCSA must meet the primary-care and sole fixed-fee conditions in IRS Notice 2026-5, question 20 . Question 19 generally permits substantiated HSA reimbursement before qualifying DPCSA coverage begins. Question 18 excludes employer-paid DPCSA fees, including fees paid through salary reduction. That exclusion concerns payment of the DPCSA fee and does not prohibit reimbursement merely because an employer contributed money to the HSA.
